She's pregnant, and he figures his part starts when labor does.

A lot of us think that. When I asked moms for the book what they wished someone had told their husbands, most of them wrote about the months before labor instead.

Ask her this week, "What will you need from me that you might not be able to say?" and write down what she tells you, so he can act on it when she can't explain.

slides.headline: What moms wish he knew while she's pregnant
slides.body: I asked birth mothers what they wished someone had told their partner. Most of them wrote about the months before labor.

slides.headline: In labor, she may not have the words
slides.body: So learn what she needs now, while she can still tell you. Ask where she wants your hands and what she wants to hear. Write it down.

slides.headline: "To anticipate needs I didn't know how to express."
slides.body: One mom, on what she wished someone had told her husband. You can't read her mind at 3 a.m. You can do the homework at dinner.

slides.headline: Go to the appointments
slides.body: That's where you learn enough to ask good questions. At our first two births, nobody told me my role, and I didn't know enough to ask.

slides.headline: Say your doubts out loud
slides.body: Then take them to the midwife together. A question answered in month six beats one that shows on your face at hour ten.

slides.headline: Plan the weeks after, too
slides.body: Who cooks and who takes nights. The birth is one night. Her recovery takes a lot longer, and she'll need you for all of it.

slides.headline: The one page that gives him a clear job
slides.body: In the back of Before the Room there's a page for her birth rules: the things she wants kept, no matter what.

slides.headline: Her rules, in her words
slides.body: Lights low. No phones. No family updates until the baby's here. Whatever matters to her, written down before labor starts.

slides.headline: In labor, she won't want to explain twice
slides.body: Kaelah, a mom from our survey, told me "it was really hard for me to talk, especially towards the end because I was so tired."

slides.headline: He keeps the rules
slides.body: Rowan, a dad I interviewed, called himself the sheriff at his wife's home birth. "I enforce the rules, 'cause we've discussed between me and Genine what the rules are."

slides.headline: Sit down and write hers

slides.headline: Have these talks before labor, not during
slides.body: Most of the work of a home birth is conversation. These are the ones I'd make sure a couple has.

slides.headline: Why does she want a home birth?
slides.body: Ask, then listen to the whole answer before you give yours. "Tell me more" gets you further than any argument.

slides.headline: What scares each of you?
slides.body: Both of you get a turn. Fears that need facts go to the midwife. Fears that need comfort stay between the two of you.

slides.headline: Who's in the room, and who gets a call?
slides.body: Decide together. Then tell family now, kindly, so nobody is surprised at the front door during labor.

slides.headline: What happens the week after?
slides.body: Who cooks, who takes nights, how long visitors stay. The midwife packs up and goes home. You'll want this settled before she does.

slides.headline: One talk a week, at a calm time
slides.body: Skip bedtime after a long day. Let her go first. Write both answers side by side so nobody has to remember who said what.

slides.headline: She's 36 weeks and he's just getting started
slides.body: He's not too late. He just has to spend the time well. Here's where I'd put it.

slides.headline: Test-run the birth space now
slides.body: Set up the room and test-fill the pool. Our water heater was drained the night Amani was born, and the tub wouldn't fill fast enough.

slides.headline: Learn the on-call list cold
slides.body: Midwife, backup, doula, whoever has the kids. Ask the midwife when she wants to hear from you once labor starts, and write it down.

slides.headline: Settle the hospital plan before labor
slides.body: Which hospital, the route, the bag. Kaelah, a mom who transferred, wished she had "planned for the worst case scenario so that I would have known what I was going into."

slides.headline: Take the house off her plate
slides.body: Meals, laundry, and the family texts asking "anything yet?" Every job you take is rest she gets back.

slides.headline: Go straight to Chapter 5
slides.body: Then the back pages of Before the Room: her birth rules, who's on call, the transfer plan, the last week. Come back for the rest after.

slides.headline: The page nobody else has to read
slides.body: Every chapter of the workbook has a page just for him. Nobody reads it, so he can write the honest answer.

slides.headline: What am I actually afraid of?
slides.body: The one that keeps him up at night. Once it's on paper, he can decide which fears go to the midwife.

slides.headline: "I had reservations but I voiced them all."
slides.body: One dad from our survey, on his wife's home birth. Writing them down first makes it easier to say them out loud.

slides.headline: At our hospital births, I never asked
slides.body: Nobody told me my role, and I didn't know enough to ask. When Amani was born at home, I knew where to be, and Katie knew I'd be there.

slides.headline: Bring one line to her
slides.body: Pick one thing from his page and say it to her. A fear she knows about is one you can plan for together.

slides.headline: Questions he should ask the midwife out loud
slides.body: Bring a written list to the next prenatal visit. Ask every question yourself, and write down what she says.

slides.headline: "When do you want us to call you?"
slides.body: Once labor starts, she'll tell you when she wants to hear from you and how. Don't guess, and don't wait for labor to find out.

slides.headline: "Which hospital, and when would you transfer?"
slides.body: Know her answer before labor. Then learn the route and how long the drive takes at night.

slides.headline: "Where do you want me during labor?"
slides.body: She's watched a lot of dads in a lot of birth rooms. Let her tell you where she'd like you, and what would help her.

slides.headline: Don't sit in the back row
slides.body: Mary, our doula, has attended more than 150 births. Her advice to partners: "Don't take a back seat role. Put yourselves upfront for the best experience."
